title: Deep multi-task learning: a review of concepts, methods, and cross-domain applications
venue: International Journal of Data Science and Analytics
themes: multi-task learning, deep learning, parameter sharing, cross-domain applications
problem: Existing reviews of multi-task learning are fragmented along individual domains and are not current with deep MTL developments, leaving the field without a unified cross-domain account of its concepts, methods, and applications.
proposed_solution: The authors present a comprehensive survey that explains MTL fundamentals, compares hard and soft parameter sharing, categorizes MTL architectures, analyzes the factors behind MTL success, and classifies application studies across a wide range of fields.
claim: The review concludes that multi-task learning is a rapidly growing and versatile paradigm that improves generalization and data efficiency across diverse domains, while its success depends on task selection, parameter-sharing architecture, and loss balancing, and it still faces challenges such as negative transfer and computational cost.
dataset_testbed: Scopus bibliographic database records of multi-task learning publications (8,245 retrieved, 6,872 unique records retained, 2020 to mid-2025)
abstract: Multi-task learning (MTL) is a machine learning method that has witnessed exponential traction due to its ability to solve multiple tasks simultaneously. Joining training-related tasks in MTL improves both predictive performance and data efficiency. The shared knowledge across tasks enables MTL models to outperform traditional single-task models. The effectiveness of MTL depends on several factors, including how tasks are chosen, how relationships between them are structured, and the choice of shared and task-specific model components. In literature, several architectures and strategies for multi-task learning have been successfully applied across different fields such as natural language processing, computer vision, healthcare, and others. However, MTL has some challenges, such as task interference, data availability, optimal task selection, and hyperparameter tuning. Recent research has introduced new techniques to address these issues, such as adaptive task balancing and parameter sharing mechanisms, although each approach has its limitations. In this review, we provide a comprehensive examination of the multi-task learning concept, and the strategies used in several different domains. It also explores the key factors influencing the success of MTL and provides a detailed classification of research efforts applying MTL in a wide range of fields, highlighting existing achievements and challenges.

title: GCond: Gradient Conflict Resolution via Accumulation-Based Stabilization for Large-Scale Multi-Task Learning
venue: IEEE Access
themes: multi-task learning, gradient conflict resolution, self-supervised learning, medical imaging
problem: In multi-task learning, gradient conflicts degrade performance, while existing resolution methods fail to scale because they require excessive memory and compute on noisy single mini-batches.
proposed_solution: The authors propose Gradient Conductor, which accumulates gradients across micro-batches to reduce variance before applying an adaptive multi-zone arbitration mechanism to resolve conflicts.
claim: GCond resolves gradient conflicts efficiently across medical CT and ImageNet benchmarks, achieving a two-fold stochastic speedup and scaling to large models where prior methods fail.
dataset_testbed: Combined head and neck CT dataset from RSNA Intracranial Hemorrhage Detection, RSNA Cervical Spine Fracture Detection, and RADCURE (2,199,444 DICOM files), ImageNet-1k (ILSVRC 2012, benjamin-paine/imagenet-1k-256x256 version), NVIDIA RTX 4080 GPU (16 GB VRAM), NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPU (32 GB VRAM), NVIDIA H200 GPU (140 GB VRAM)
abstract: In multi-task learning (MTL), gradient conflict poses a significant challenge. Effective methods for addressing this problem, including PCGrad, CAGrad, and GradNorm, in their original implementations are computationally demanding, which significantly limits their application in modern large models such as transformers. We propose Gradient Conductor (GCond), a method that builds upon PCGrad principles by combining them with gradient accumulation and an adaptive arbitration mechanism. We evaluated GCond on self-supervised multi-task learning tasks using MobileNetV3-Small and ConvNeXt architectures on the ImageNet 1K dataset and a combined head and neck CT scan dataset, comparing the proposed method against baseline linear combinations and state-of-the-art gradient conflict resolution methods. The classical and stochastic approaches of GCond were analyzed. The stochastic mode of GCond achieved a two-fold computational speedup while maintaining optimization quality, and demonstrated superior performance across all evaluated metrics, achieving lower L1 and SSIM losses compared to other methods on both datasets, and demonstrating superior generalization in heterogeneous scenarios: GCond improved ImageNet Top-1 Accuracy by 4.5% over baselines and prevented confidence overfitting in medical diagnosis tasks. GCond exhibited high scalability, being successfully applied to both compact models: MobileNetV3-Small and ConvNeXt-tiny; and large architecture ConvNeXtV2-Base. It also showed compatibility with modern optimizers such as AdamW and Lion/LARS. Therefore, GCond offers a scalable and efficient solution to the problem of gradient conflicts in multi-task learning.

title: Resolving Token-Space Gradient Conflicts: Token Space Manipulation for Transformer-Based Multi-Task Learning
venue: Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV 2025)
themes: multi-task learning, vision transformers, negative transfer, gradient conflict
problem: Conflicting objectives among tasks cause negative transfer in multi-task learning, while the fixed capacity and rigid structure of pre-trained transformers limit model adaptability.
proposed_solution: The authors propose DTME-MTL, which decomposes token space using singular value decomposition and mitigates negative transfer through affine token modulation and task-specific token expansion.
claim: DTME-MTL consistently improves multi-task performance across multiple vision benchmarks with minimal computational overhead and parameter growth by resolving gradient conflicts in token space.
dataset_testbed: NYUD-v2, PASCAL-Context, Taskonomy, NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU
abstract: Multi-Task Learning (MTL) enables multiple tasks to be learned within a shared network, but differences in objectives across tasks can cause negative transfer, where the learning of one task degrades another task’s performance. While pre-trained transformers significantly improve MTL performance, their fixed network capacity and rigid structure limit adaptability. Previous dynamic network architectures attempt to address this but are inefficient as they directly convert shared parameters into task-specific ones. We propose Dynamic Token Modulation and Expansion (DTME-MTL), a framework applicable to any transformer-based MTL architecture. DTME-MTL enhances adaptability and reduces overfitting by identifying gradient conflicts in token space and applying adaptive solutions based on conflict type. Unlike prior methods that mitigate negative transfer by duplicating network parameters, DTME-MTL operates entirely in token space, enabling efficient adaptation without excessive parameter growth. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DTME-MTL consistently improves multi-task performance with minimal computational overhead, offering a scalable and effective solution for enhancing transformer-based MTL models.

title: Dual-Balancing for Multi-Task Learning
venue: Neural Networks
themes: multi-task learning, loss balancing, gradient balancing
problem: In multi-task learning, tasks differ in loss and gradient scales, so tasks with large values can dominate model updates and leave other tasks with poor performance.
proposed_solution: The authors propose DB-MTL, which applies a logarithm transformation to each task loss for loss-scale balancing and normalizes every task gradient to the maximum gradient norm for gradient-magnitude balancing.
claim: Balancing both loss scales and gradient magnitudes lets DB-MTL consistently outperform the state of the art across benchmark datasets.
dataset_testbed: NYUv2, Cityscapes, QM9, Office-31, Office-Home, NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 GPU
abstract: Multi-task learning aims to learn multiple related tasks simultaneously and has achieved great success in various fields. However, the disparity in loss and gradient scales among tasks often leads to performance compromises, and the balancing of tasks remains a significant challenge. In this paper, we propose Dual-Balancing Multi-Task Learning (DB-MTL) to achieve task balancing from both the loss and gradient perspectives. Specifically, DB-MTL achieves loss-scale balancing by performing logarithm transformation on each task loss, and rescales gradient magnitudes by normalizing all task gradients to comparable magnitudes using the maximum gradient norm. Extensive experiments on a number of benchmark datasets demonstrate that DB-MTL consistently performs better than the current state-of-the-art.

title: MT2ST: Adaptive Multi-Task to Single-Task Learning
venue: Proceedings of the 1st Workshop on Multimodal Augmented Generation via Multimodal Retrieval (MAGMaR 2025)
themes: multi-task learning, training efficiency, representation learning, multimodal learning
algorithm_or_model: MT2ST with Diminish and Switch transition strategies
problem: Multi-task training helps generalization but causes gradient conflicts, task interference, and extra computation, while single-task training lacks representation reuse, so efficient training is hard to achieve.
proposed_solution: They propose MT2ST, a framework that starts with multi-task learning and then transitions to single-task optimization through decaying auxiliary weights or a scheduled hard switch.
claim: Across text, vision, and multimodal models, MT2ST improves or keeps task accuracy while cutting training time and computation by a large margin.
dataset_testbed: MNLI (GLUE), SST-2 and QQP (GLUE), VQA v2.0, Visual7W Telling, Flickr30k Entities, CIFAR-100, TinyImageNet, MS-COCO, 4x NVIDIA A100 GPUs
abstract: We propose MT2ST, a general and efficient framework for accelerating multi-task training by progressively transitioning to single-task optimization. Unlike conventional multi-task learning (MTL) or singletask fine-tuning (STL), MT2ST dynamically adjusts the training focus via two complementary strategies: Diminish, which gradually down-weights auxiliary losses, and Switch, which explicitly switches to the primary task at a scheduled point. We demonstrate the effectiveness of MT2ST across three key paradigms: representation learning, transformers, and diffusion models, covering both unimodal (text/image) and multimodal (vision-language) tasks. Extensive experiments show that MT2ST significantly improves training efficiency—achieving up to 56% FLOPs compression—while maintaining or surpassing task performance. These results suggest MT2ST as a general-purpose solution for scalable and adaptive multi-task training. Although this work is general-purpose, it is especially suitable for multimodal settings such as VQA or vision-language retrieval, where auxiliary pretraining (e.g., masked language modeling or contrastive learning) often diverges from final objectives. We include a VQA case study and outline its efficiency for multimodal retrieval in §4.

title: FiLLM - A Filipino-optimized Large Language Model based on Southeast Asia Large Language Model (SEALLM)
venue: arXiv
themes: low-resource language NLP, large language models, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, Filipino language processing
algorithm_or_model: FiLLM, a LoRA fine-tuned SeaLLM-7B 2.5 model
problem: Large language models for the Filipino language remain underdeveloped because labeled Filipino datasets and computational resources are scarce.
proposed_solution: The authors build FiLLM by applying LoRA fine-tuning to the SeaLLM-7B 2.5 model on Filipino datasets, then compare it with CalamanCy on several NLP tasks.
claim: FiLLM performs well on Named Entity Recognition and Part-of-Speech tagging, but CalamanCy significantly outperforms it overall, especially on Dependency Parsing.
dataset_testbed: Filipino Hatespeech Dataset (10,000 tweets), Filipino Dengue Dataset (4,000 tweets), TLUnified-NER Dataset, Merged UD Dataset (Ugnayan and TRG treebanks), Asian Language Treebank, NewsPHNLI Dataset
abstract: This study presents FiLLM, a Filipino-optimized large language model, designed to enhance natural language processing (NLP) capabilities in the Filipino language. Built upon the SeaLLM-7B 2.5 model, FiLLM leverages Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) finetuning to optimize memory efficiency while maintaining taskspecific performance. The model was trained and evaluated on diverse Filipino datasets to address key NLP tasks, including Named Entity Recognition (NER), Part-of-Speech (POS) tagging, Dependency Parsing, and Text Summarization. Performance comparisons with the CalamanCy model were conducted using F1 Score, Precision, Recall, Compression Rate, and Keyword Overlap metrics. Results indicate that Calamancy outperforms FILLM in several aspects, demonstrating its effectiveness in processing Filipino text with improved linguistic comprehension and adaptability. This research contributes to the advancement of Filipino NLP applications by providing an optimized, efficient, and scalable language model tailored for local linguistic needs.

title: FilBench: Can LLMs Understand and Generate Filipino?
venue: EMNLP 2025 main
themes: large language models, benchmark evaluation, low-resource languages, machine translation
problem: Existing LLM benchmarks either exclude Filipino and other Philippine languages or lack the task and language diversity needed to measure how well models handle them.
proposed_solution: The authors curate FilBench, a benchmark with four task categories and twelve subtasks built from expert-annotated Filipino, Tagalog, and Cebuano datasets, and use it to evaluate 27 state-of-the-art LLMs.
claim: FilBench is difficult even for leading models, since GPT-4o tops it at only 72.23 percent, the best Southeast Asian-focused model reaches 61.07 percent, and generation tasks are the weakest area across models.
dataset_testbed: FilBench, Dengue Filipino, BalitaNLP, SIB-200, CebuaNER, TLUnified-NER, Universal NER, FiReCS, INCLUDE, Global MMLU, KALAHI, StingrayBench, Cebuano Readability Corpus, Belebele, NewsPH NLI, NTREX-128, Tatoeba, TICO-19
abstract: Despite the impressive performance of LLMs on English-based tasks, little is known about their capabilities in specific languages such as Filipino. In this work, we address this gap by introducing FilBench, a Filipino-centric benchmark designed to evaluate LLMs across a diverse set of tasks and capabilities in Filipino, Tagalog, and Cebuano. We carefully curate the tasks in FilBench to reflect the priorities and trends of NLP research in the Philippines such as Cultural Knowledge, Classical NLP, Reading Comprehension, and Generation. By evaluating 27 state-of-the-art LLMs on FilBench, we find that several LLMs suffer from reading comprehension and translation capabilities. Our results indicate that FilBench is challenging, with the best model, GPT-4o, achieving only a score of 72.23%. Moreover, we also find that models trained specifically for Southeast Asian languages tend to underperform on FilBench, with the highest-performing model, SEA-LION v3 70B, achieving only a score of 61.07%. Our work demonstrates the value of curating language-specific LLM benchmarks to aid in driving progress on Filipino NLP and increasing the inclusion of Philippine languages in LLM development.

title: Multi-objective Deep Learning: Taxonomy and Survey of the State of the Art
venue: Machine Learning with Applications
themes: multi-objective optimization, deep learning, multi-task learning, multi-objective reinforcement learning
problem: Training deep neural networks under several conflicting objectives is attractive but very expensive, and the fast growth of publications makes the field difficult to navigate.
proposed_solution: The authors organize existing work in a taxonomy based on the type of training algorithm and the decision maker's needs, and survey methods across all learning paradigms plus applications.
claim: The authors argue that considering multiple conflicting criteria will become the standard in deep learning and that gradient-based methods such as MGDA have emerged as the dominant approach.
dataset_testbed: N/A
abstract: Simultaneously considering multiple objectives in machine learning has been a popular approach for several decades, with various benefits for multi-task learning, the consideration of secondary goals such as sparsity, or multicriteria hyperparameter tuning. However—as multi-objective optimization is significantly more costly than single-objective optimization—the recent focus on deep learning architectures poses considerable additional challenges due to the very large number of parameters, strong nonlinearities and stochasticity. This survey covers recent advancements in the area of multi-objective deep learning. We introduce a taxonomy of existing methods—based on the type of training algorithm as well as the decision maker's needs—before listing recent advancements, and also successful applications. All three main learning paradigms supervised learning, unsupervised learning and reinforcement learning are covered, and we also address the recently very popular area of generative modeling.

title: Beyond Losses Reweighting: Empowering Multi-Task Learning via the Generalization Perspective
venue: Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV)
themes: multi-task learning, sharpness-aware minimization, loss landscape flatness, gradient conflict
algorithm_or_model: Flat-based (F-) variants of gradient-based MTL methods, such as F-MGDA, F-PCGrad, F-CAGrad, F-IMTL, F-NashMTL, and F-FairGrad
problem: Existing gradient manipulation methods for multi-task learning minimize only empirical losses and ignore loss landscape geometry, so shared models overfit and task gradients conflict with each other.
proposed_solution: The paper proposes a sharpness-aware framework that penalizes each task sharpness through weight perturbation and aggregates separate loss and flatness gradients on top of existing gradient manipulation methods.
claim: Adding sharpness-aware flat minima seeking to gradient-based multi-task learning methods improves task performance, robustness, and calibration across image classification and scene understanding benchmarks.
dataset_testbed: Multi-MNIST (MultiFashion, MultiMNIST, MultiFashion+MNIST), CelebA, NYUv2, CityScapes
abstract: Multi-task learning (MTL) trains deep neural networks to optimize several objectives simultaneously using a shared backbone, which leads to reduced computational costs, improved data efficiency, and enhanced performance through cross-task knowledge sharing. Although recent gradient manipulation techniques aim to find a common descent direction that benefits all tasks, conventional empirical loss minimization still leaves models vulnerable to overfitting and gradient conflicts. To address this, we introduce a novel MTL framework that leverages weight perturbation to regulate gradient norms, thus improving generalization. By carefully modulating weight perturbations, our approach harmonizes task-specific gradients, reducing conflicts and encouraging more robust learning across tasks. Theoretical insights reveal that controlling the gradient norm through weight perturbation directly contributes to better generalization. Extensive experiments across diverse applications demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing gradientbased MTL techniques in terms of task performance and overall model robustness.

title: NTKMTL: Mitigating Task Imbalance in Multi-Task Learning from Neural Tangent Kernel Perspective
venue: arXiv
themes: multi-task learning, task imbalance, neural tangent kernel, loss weighting
problem: Task imbalance in multi-task learning, where some tasks dominate training while others are under-optimized, persists because accurately characterizing the training dynamics and convergence speeds of multiple tasks within a complex MTL system is very difficult, and prior loss-scale-based approximations fail to capture true convergence behavior.
proposed_solution: The authors extend Neural Tangent Kernel theory to MTL by introducing an extended NTK matrix whose spectral analysis reveals task-level convergence speeds, and propose NTKMTL, which normalizes the maximum eigenvalues of per-task NTK matrices to set task weights, plus an efficient shared-representation approximation NTKMTL-SR.
claim: By using NTK spectral analysis to balance per-task convergence speeds, NTKMTL and NTKMTL-SR achieve state-of-the-art or competitive performance across supervised benchmarks with 2 to 40 tasks and multi-task reinforcement learning, with NTKMTL obtaining the best performance drop on NYUv2, CityScapes, and CelebA.
dataset_testbed: NYUv2, CityScapes, QM9, CelebA, Meta-World MT10
abstract: Multi-Task Learning (MTL) enables a single model to learn multiple tasks simultaneously, leveraging knowledge transfer among tasks for enhanced generalization, and has been widely applied across various domains. However, task imbalance remains a major challenge in MTL. Although balancing the convergence speeds of different tasks is an effective approach to address this issue, it is highly challenging to accurately characterize the training dynamics and convergence speeds of multiple tasks within the complex MTL system. To this end, we attempt to analyze the training dynamics in MTL by leveraging Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) theory and propose a new MTL method, NTKMTL. Specifically, we introduce an extended NTK matrix for MTL and adopt spectral analysis to balance the convergence speeds of multiple tasks, thereby mitigating task imbalance. Based on the approximation via shared representation, we further propose NTKMTL-SR, achieving training efficiency while maintaining competitive performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our methods achieve state-of-the-art performance across a wide range of benchmarks, including both multi-task supervised learning and multi-task reinforcement learning. Source code is available at [https://github.com/jianke0604/NTKMTL](https://github.com/jianke0604/NTKMTL "").

title: COMI-LINGUA: Expert Annotated Large-Scale Dataset for Multitask NLP in Hindi-English Code-Mixing
venue: arXiv
themes: code-mixing, Hindi-English NLP, dataset annotation, large language models
algorithm_or_model: COMI-LINGUA dataset with LoRA fine-tuned open-weight LLMs (LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, aya-expanse-8b, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct)
problem: Existing Hindi-English (Hinglish) code-mixed resources are small, skewed toward the Roman script, narrow in task coverage, and often synthetically generated rather than human-annotated, leaving researchers without a large, high-quality benchmark for training and evaluating models on code-mixed NLP.
proposed_solution: The authors curate COMI-LINGUA, the largest expert-annotated Hinglish code-mixed dataset spanning five NLP tasks and both Devanagari and Roman scripts, and use it to benchmark traditional NLP tools and LLMs under zero-shot, one-shot, and fine-tuned settings.
claim: Fine-tuning open-weight LLMs on COMI-LINGUA brings substantial gains over prompting approaches and traditional tools, setting new benchmarks for Hinglish code-mixed NLP with up to 98.77 F1 on MLI and 95.25 F1 on NER.
dataset_testbed: COMI-LINGUA (newly created expert-annotated Hinglish code-mixed dataset, 125,615 instances across five tasks), raw text scraped from Indian news portals, X (Twitter), YouTube, and government archives, plus supplementary Hinglish samples from prior corpora (e.g., PHINC), four NVIDIA Tesla V100 32 GB GPUs for fine-tuning and inference
abstract: We introduce COMI-LINGUA, the largest manually annotated Hindi-English code-mixed dataset, comprising 125K+ high-quality instances across five core NLP tasks: Token-level Language Identification, Matrix Language Identification, Named Entity Recognition, Part-Of-Speech Tagging and Machine Translation. Each instance is annotated by three bilingual annotators, yielding over 376K expert annotations with strong inter-annotator agreement (Fleiss’ Kappa ≥\\geq 0.81). The rigorously preprocessed and filtered dataset covers both Devanagari and Roman scripts and spans diverse domains, ensuring real-world linguistic coverage. Evaluation reveals that closed-weight LLMs significantly outperform traditional tools and open-weight models in zero-shot settings. Notably, one-shot prompting consistently boosts performance across tasks, especially in structure-sensitive predictions like POS and NER. Fine-tuning open-weight LLMs on COMI-LINGUA demonstrates substantial improvements, achieving up to 95.25 F1 in NER, 98.77 F1 in MLI, and competitive MT performance, setting new benchmarks for Hinglish code-mixed text. COMI-LINGUA is publicly available at this URL11 1 [https://huggingface.co/datasets/LingoIITGN/COMI-LINGUA](https://huggingface.co/datasets/LingoIITGN/COMI-LINGUA "") Version 1.0, Updated till 15nd September 2025..

title: Beyond Monolingual Assumptions: A Survey on Code-Switched NLP in the Era of Large Language Models across Modalities
venue: arXiv
themes: code-switching, large language models, multilingual NLP, multimodal NLP
problem: Large language models struggle with mixed-language inputs due to scarce code-switching datasets, evaluation biases, and monolingual training assumptions.
proposed_solution: The authors present a comprehensive survey of code-switched NLP research in the LLM era, covering architectures, training strategies, evaluation methods, and a future roadmap.
claim: The authors find that LLM gains in code-switching remain limited to high-resource languages, while models still struggle in low-resource settings.
dataset_testbed: N/A
abstract: Amidst the rapid advances of large language models (LLMs), most LLMs still struggle with mixed-language inputs, limited Code-switching (CSW) datasets, and evaluation biases, which hinder their deployment in multilingual societies. This survey provides the first comprehensive analysis of CSW-aware LLM research, reviewing ?​??? studies spanning five research areas, 15+ NLP tasks, 30+ datasets, and 80+ languages. We categorize recent advances by architecture, training strategy, and evaluation methodology, outlining how LLMs have reshaped CSW modeling and identifying the challenges that persist. The paper concludes with a roadmap that emphasizes the need for inclusive datasets, fair evaluation, and linguistically grounded models to achieve truly multilingual capabilities.11 1 A curated collection of all resources is maintained at [https://github.com/lingo-iitgn/awesome-code-mixing/](https://github.com/lingo-iitgn/awesome-code-mixing/ "").

title: HiligayNER: A Baseline Named Entity Recognition Model for Hiligaynon
venue: Pacific Asia Conference on Language, Information and Computation
themes: named entity recognition, low-resource languages, Philippine languages, cross-lingual transfer
algorithm_or_model: HiligayNER, fine-tuned mBERT and XLM-RoBERTa token classifiers
problem: Hiligaynon, a regional Philippine language spoken by over 10 million people, has no publicly available NER corpus or baseline model, which leaves it underrepresented in language processing research.
proposed_solution: The authors compiled an annotated corpus of over 8,000 Hiligaynon sentences with BIO entity tags and fine-tuned mBERT and XLM-RoBERTa on it to create baseline NER models.
claim: Both finetuned models exceed 0.80 F1 on all main entity tags, and zero-shot transfer to Cebuano and Tagalog reaches about 0.46 macro F1, showing cross-lingual utility.
dataset_testbed: HiligayNER corpus of 8,082 cleaned Hiligaynon sentences collected from online news articles, social media posts, and literary texts, Cebuano test data for zero-shot cross-lingual evaluation, Tagalog test data for zero-shot cross-lingual evaluation
abstract: The language of Hiligaynon, spoken predominantly by the people of Panay Island, Negros Occidental, and Soccsksargen in the Philippines, remains underrepresented in language processing research due to the absence of annotated corpora and baseline models. This study introduces HiligayNER, the first publicly available baseline model for the task of Named Entity Recognition (NER) in Hiligaynon. The dataset used to build HiligayNER contains over 8,000 annotated sentences collected from publicly available news articles, social media posts, and literary texts. Two Transformer-based models, mBERT and XLM-RoBERTa, were fine-tuned on this collected corpus to build versions of HiligayNER. Evaluation results show strong performance, with both models achieving over 80% in precision, recall, and F1-score across entity types. Furthermore, cross-lingual evaluation with Cebuano and Tagalog demonstrates promising transferability, suggesting the broader applicability of HiligayNER for multilingual NLP in low-resource settings. This work aims to contribute to language technology development for underrepresented Philippine languages, specifically for Hiligaynon, and support future research in regional language processing.

title: Injecting Imbalance Sensitivity for Multi-Task Learning
venue: Proceedings of the Thirty-Fourth International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI-25)
themes: multi-task learning, gradient manipulation, task imbalance, multi-objective optimization
problem: Gradient-based optimization methods for multi-task learning concentrate on resolving conflicting task gradients while neglecting the imbalance or dominance among individual task gradients, which the authors argue is the more significant obstacle to optimizing all tasks simultaneously.
proposed_solution: The authors inject imbalance sensitivity into an established gradient-combination baseline (CAGrad) by adding a projected-norm constraint that encourages the combined gradient to promote every individual task, with an adaptive weighting tied to a cosine-based measure of gradient imbalance, and apply the same idea to augment Nash-MTL.
claim: Adding imbalance sensitivity lets IMGrad consistently improve its gradient-manipulation baselines and surpass prior state-of-the-art gradient manipulation methods across supervised and reinforcement learning benchmarks, including the best overall ∆m% on NYUv2 and CityScapes and the highest success rate on MT10.
dataset_testbed: CityScapes, NYUv2, CelebA, MT10 (Meta-World), imbalanced synthetic two-task toy benchmark, Tesla V100 GPUs
abstract: Multi-task learning (MTL) has emerged as a promising approach for deploying deep learning models in real-life applications. Recent studies have proposed optimization-based learning paradigms to establish task-shared representations in MTL. However, our paper empirically argues that these studies, specifically gradient-based ones, primarily emphasize the conflict issue while neglecting the potentially more significant impact of imbalance/dominance in MTL. In line with this perspective, we enhance the existing baseline method by injecting imbalance-sensitivity through the imposition of constraints on the projected norms. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed IMbalance-sensitive Gradient (IMGrad) descent method, we evaluate it on multiple mainstream MTL benchmarks, encompassing supervised learning tasks as well as reinforcement learning. The experimental results consistently demonstrate competitive performance.

title: Multi-Task Learning in Natural Language Processing: An Overview
venue: ACM Computing Surveys
themes: multi-task learning, natural language processing, deep learning, model architectures
problem: Directly training deep neural models on NLP tasks suffers from pervasive overfitting and data scarcity, because sufficiently training such models requires large amounts of expensive labeled data along with substantial computing, time, and storage budgets.
proposed_solution: The authors survey how multi-task learning is applied to NLP by organizing MTL architectures into four classes (parallel, hierarchical, modular, and generative adversarial) and reviewing optimization techniques for loss construction, gradient regularization, data sampling, and task scheduling, along with applications and benchmark datasets.
claim: The survey provides a structured taxonomy of multi-task learning in NLP, arguing that learning from multiple related tasks lets models aggregate training data, share common knowledge, and achieve simultaneous performance improvements across tasks, while identifying task relatedness, leveraging unlabeled data, and better MTL architectures for pre-trained language models as key open directions.
dataset_testbed: N/A
abstract: Deep learning approaches have achieved great success in the field of Natural Language Processing (NLP). However, directly training deep neural models often suffer from overfitting and data scarcity problems that are pervasive in NLP tasks. In recent years, Multi-Task Learning (MTL), which can leverage useful information of related tasks to achieve simultaneous performance improvement on these tasks, has been used to handle these problems. In this paper, we give an overview of the use of MTL in NLP tasks. We first review MTL architectures used in NLP tasks and categorize them into four classes, including parallel architecture, hierarchical architecture, modular architecture, and generative adversarial architecture. Then we present optimization techniques on loss construction, gradient regularization, data sampling, and task scheduling to properly train a multi-task model. After presenting applications of MTL in a variety of NLP tasks, we introduce some benchmark datasets. Finally, we make a conclusion and discuss several possible research directions in this field.

title: Careful with that Scalpel: Improving Gradient Surgery with an EMA
venue: International Conference on Machine Learning
themes: gradient surgery, bilevel optimization, multi-task learning, auxiliary losses
problem: Training with an auxiliary loss often fails because curvature conflicts and stochastic gradient noise degrade optimization in standard regularized and gradient surgery methods.
proposed_solution: The authors propose Bloop, which updates parameters along the main gradient plus the auxiliary gradient projected orthogonal to an exponential moving average of past main gradients.
claim: Using an exponential moving average of main gradients in gradient surgery improves trade-offs between main and auxiliary losses over existing methods across vision and language tasks.
dataset_testbed: MNIST (MLP trained with a Lipschitz constant proxy as auxiliary loss), ImageNet (ResNet50 trained with squared L2 norm auxiliary loss), Cifar10Mnist (composite of CIFAR-10 and MNIST, ResNet18 with two classification heads), C4 (30M examples for next-token prediction pre-training), RCV-1 (20K examples as the auxiliary specialization dataset), Paracrawl (36M English-German sentence pairs for the main translation loss), WMT (2009-2019 data as auxiliary translation set, 2020 data for evaluation), CIFAR-10 (joint classification with ImageNet in the appendix experiment)
abstract: Beyond minimizing a single training loss, many deep learning estimation pipelines rely on an auxiliary objective to quantify and encourage desirable properties of the model (e.g. performance on another dataset, robustness, agreement with a prior). Although the simplest approach to incorporating an auxiliary loss is to sum it with the training loss as a regularizer, recent works have shown that one can improve performance by blending the gradients beyond a simple sum; this is known as gradient surgery. We cast the problem as a constrained minimization problem where the auxiliary objective is minimized among the set of minimizers of the training loss. To solve this bilevel problem, we follow a parameter update direction that combines the training loss gradient and the orthogonal projection of the auxiliary gradient to the training gradient. In a setting where gradients come from mini-batches, we explain how, using a moving average of the training loss gradients, we can carefully maintain this critical orthogonality property. We demonstrate that our method, Bloop, can lead to much better performances on NLP and vision experiments than other gradient surgery methods without EMA.

title: Quantifying Task Priority for Multi-Task Optimization
venue: Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR)
themes: multi-task learning, multi-task optimization, conflicting gradients, dense prediction
problem: Gradient manipulation methods realign conflicting gradients without knowing which shared parameters matter for each task, so multi-task learning ends at sub-optimal Pareto solutions with negative transfer.
proposed_solution: The authors quantify task priority with the strength of task-specific connections and split optimization into a phase that learns the priority and a phase that projects gradients to preserve it.
claim: Learning and preserving task priority enables the method to find new Pareto optimal solutions and to consistently outperform earlier gradient manipulation methods on multiple datasets, loss scalings, and architectures.
dataset_testbed: NYUD-v2, PASCAL-Context, Cityscapes
abstract: The goal of multi-task learning is to learn diverse tasks within a single unified network. As each task has its own unique objective function, conflicts emerge during training, resulting in negative transfer among them. Earlier research identified these conflicting gradients in shared parameters between tasks and attempted to realign them in the same direction. However, we prove that such optimization strategies lead to sub-optimal Pareto solutions due to their inability to accurately determine the individual contributions of each parameter across various tasks. In this paper, we propose the concept of task priority to evaluate parameter contributions across different tasks. To learn task priority, we identify the type of connections related to links between parameters influenced by task-specific losses during backpropagation. The strength of connections is gauged by the magnitude of parameters to determine task priority. Based on these, we present a new method named connection strength-based optimization for multi-task learning which consists of two phases. The first phase learns the task priority within the network, while the second phase modifies the gradients while upholding this priority. This ultimately leads to finding new Pareto optimal solutions for multiple tasks. Through extensive experiments, we show that our approach greatly enhances multi-task performance in comparison to earlier gradient manipulation methods.

title: Zero-Shot Classification of Crisis Tweets Using Instruction-Finetuned Large Language Models
venue: IEEE IHTC 2024 (Int. Humanitarian Technologies Conference)
themes: zero-shot classification, large language models, crisis informatics, social media
algorithm_or_model: Zero-shot classification with instruction-tuned LLMs, specifically GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5 Flash, and Claude 3.5 Sonnet
problem: Humanitarian practitioners lack knowledge of how well commercial large language models classify crisis social media posts without task-specific training, and of how such zero-shot performance compares to fine-tuned benchmarks.
proposed_solution: They prompt three commercial models in a single instruction to judge informativeness and rank 16 humanitarian labels, then score the zero-shot answers on CrisisBench across prompt configurations.
claim: Zero-shot LLMs come within six percent of fine-tuned classifiers on the binary informativeness task, while performance drops sharply on the 16-class humanitarian task mostly because of ambiguous dataset labels.
dataset_testbed: CrisisBench consolidated crisis tweet dataset, CrisisMMD image tweet subset within CrisisBench, Manually annotated sample of 225 tweets from the affected_individual, caution_and_advice, and disease_related classes
abstract: Social media posts are frequently identified as a valuable source of open-source intelligence for disaster response, and pre-LLM NLP techniques have been evaluated on datasets of crisis tweets. We assess three commercial large language models (OpenAI GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5-flash-001 and Anthropic Claude-3-5 Sonnet) capabilities in zero-shot classification of short social media posts. In one prompt, the models are asked to perform two classification tasks: 1) identify if the post is informative in a humanitarian context; and 2) rank and provide probabilities for the post in relation to 16 possible humanitarian classes. The posts being classified are from the consolidated crisis tweet dataset, CrisisBench. Results are evaluated using macro, weighted, and binary F1-scores. The informative classification task, generally performed better without extra information, while for the humanitarian label classification providing the event that occurred during which the tweet was mined, resulted in better performance. Further, we found that the models have significantly varying performance by dataset, which raises questions about dataset quality.

title: Kalahi: A handcrafted, grassroots cultural LLM evaluation suite for Filipino
venue: PACLIC 38 (2024)
themes: cultural evaluation of LLMs, Filipino NLP, benchmark datasets, low-resource languages
problem: Current multilingual LLMs often fail to give culturally fitting answers to Filipino users because most cultural evaluations are built top-down from large surveys and translated English datasets.
proposed_solution: The authors built Kalahi, a set of 150 handcrafted Filipino situation prompts with culturally relevant and irrelevant answer options, written and validated together with native Filipino speakers.
claim: Native Filipino validators answered most Kalahi items correctly while the best of nine tested LLMs reached only 46.0 percent, so the benchmark reliably measures Filipino cultural representation in LLMs.
dataset_testbed: Kalahi (new 150-prompt handcrafted Filipino cultural evaluation suite), Aya 23 8B, Qwen 2 7B Instruct, Sailor 7B Chat, SeaLLMs 3 7B Chat, BLOOMZ 7B1, Falcon 7B Instruct, Gemma 2 9B Instruct, Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, SEA-LION 2.1 8B Instruct
abstract: Multilingual large language models (LLMs) today may not necessarily provide culturally appropriate and relevant responses to its Filipino users. We introduce Kalahi, a cultural LLM evaluation suite that is part of SEA-HELM. It was collaboratively created by native Filipino speakers, and is composed of 150 high-quality, handcrafted and nuanced prompts that test LLMs for generations that are relevant to shared Filipino cultural knowledge and values. Strong LLM performance in Kalahi indicates a model's ability to generate responses similar to what an average Filipino would say or do in a given situation. We conducted experiments on LLMs with multilingual and Filipino language support. Results show that Kalahi, while trivial for Filipinos, is challenging for LLMs, with the best model answering only 46.0% of the questions correctly compared to native Filipino performance of 89.10%. Thus, Kalahi can be used to accurately and reliably evaluate Filipino cultural representation in LLMs.

title: Proactive Gradient Conflict Mitigation in Multi-Task Learning: A Sparse Training Perspective
venue: arXiv
themes: multi-task learning, gradient conflict, sparse training, parameter selection
algorithm_or_model: Sparse training (ST) with parameter selection per neuron (PSN)
problem: Gradient conflicts between task gradients during joint multi-task training cause task competition, and existing gradient manipulation methods react to conflicts without reducing how often they occur.
proposed_solution: The authors propose sparse training that updates only a selected subset of parameters chosen per neuron by magnitude, and they combine it with gradient manipulation methods.
claim: Sparse training lowers the frequency of gradient conflict during training and consistently improves multi-task performance across datasets and architectures, both alone and combined with gradient manipulation methods.
dataset_testbed: NYUv2, CityScapes, CelebA, Clevr (from VTAB), SmallNORB (from VTAB)
abstract: Advancing towards generalist agents necessitates the concurrent processing of multiple tasks using a unified model, thereby underscoring the growing significance of simultaneous model training on multiple downstream tasks. A common issue in multi-task learning is the occurrence of gradient conflict, which leads to potential competition among different tasks during joint training. This competition often results in improvements in one task at the expense of deterioration in another. Although several optimization methods have been developed to address this issue by manipulating task gradients for better task balancing, they cannot decrease the incidence of gradient conflict. In this paper, we systematically investigate the occurrence of gradient conflict across different methods and propose a strategy to reduce such conflicts through sparse training (ST), wherein only a portion of the model's parameters are updated during training while keeping the rest unchanged. Our extensive experiments demonstrate that ST effectively mitigates conflicting gradients and leads to superior performance. Furthermore, ST can be easily integrated with gradient manipulation techniques, thus enhancing their effectiveness.

title: Do All Languages Cost the Same? Tokenization in the Era of Commercial Language Models
venue: Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP 2023)
themes: tokenization, multilingual language models, commercial LM APIs, fairness
algorithm_or_model: byte-level byte pair encoding (BBPE) tokenization, analyzed on ChatGPT (gpt-3.5-turbo) and BLOOMZ
problem: Commercial language model APIs charge users per token, and because subword tokenizers fragment different languages and scripts at very different rates, speakers of some languages pay much more to convey the same information.
proposed_solution: The authors run a systematic analysis across 22 typologically diverse languages measuring tokenizer fragmentation, estimated API cost, in-context learning performance, and socio-economic affordability, to expose the unfairness of per-token API pricing.
claim: Speakers of many supported non-Latin-script languages are overcharged by commercial LM APIs while receiving poorer in-context learning performance, and this double unfairness falls hardest on populations in less economically developed countries.
dataset_testbed: FLORES-200 (subset), WMT 2021 data, XNLI, XFACT, XQUAD, CrossSum, XLSUM, CC100 (used to estimate ChatGPT pretraining language distribution), ChatGPT (gpt-3.5-turbo) via OpenAI API, BLOOMZ via HuggingFace Inference API
abstract: Language models have graduated from being research prototypes to commercialized products offered as web APIs, and recent works have highlighted the multilingual capabilities of these products. The API vendors charge their users based on usage, more specifically on the number of “tokens” processed or generated by the underlying language models. What constitutes a token, however, is training data and model dependent with a large variance in the number of tokens required to convey the same information in different languages. In this work, we analyze the effect of this non-uniformity on the fairness of an API’s pricing policy across languages. We conduct a systematic analysis of the cost and utility of OpenAI’s language model API on multilingual benchmarks in 22 typologically diverse languages. We show evidence that speakers of a large number of the supported languages are overcharged while obtaining poorer results. These speakers tend to also come from regions where the APIs are less affordable to begin with. Through these analyses, we aim to increase transparency around language model APIs’ pricing policies and encourage the vendors to make them more equitable.

title: Improving Gradient Trade-offs between Tasks in Multi-task Text Classification
venue: Proceedings of the 61st Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics Volume 1: Long Papers
themes: multi-task learning, text classification, gradient conflict, multi-objective optimization
problem: Simultaneous training of multiple tasks often degrades performance because tasks conflict with each other and existing methods achieve only arbitrary Pareto trade-offs.
proposed_solution: The authors propose GetMTL, a gradient trade-off method that optimizes update directions near the average task gradient to improve all tasks simultaneously.
claim: GetMTL outperforms existing multi-task learning methods on both benchmarks by reaching superior average classification accuracy and improving individual task performance.
dataset_testbed: Amazon Review dataset with 14 product review domains treated as 14 binary classification tasks (22180 training and 5600 test instances), Topic classification dataset from 20 Newsgroups with 16 newsgroups divided into four 4-way classification tasks
abstract: Multi-task learning (MTL) has emerged as a promising approach for sharing inductive bias across multiple tasks to enable more efficient learning in text classification. However, training all tasks simultaneously often yields degraded performance of each task than learning them independently, since different tasks might conflict with each other. Existing MTL methods for alleviating this issue is to leverage heuristics or gradient-based algorithm to achieve an arbitrary Pareto optimal trade-off among different tasks. In this paper, we present a novel gradient trade-off approach to mitigate the task conflict problem, dubbed GetMTL, which can achieve a specific tradeoff among different tasks nearby the main objective of multi-task text classification (MTC), so as to improve the performance of each task simultaneously. The results of extensive experiments on two benchmark datasets back up our theoretical analysis and validate the superiority of our proposed GetMTL.

title: TaskWeb: Selecting Better Source Tasks for Multi-task NLP
venue: Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP 2023)
themes: multi-task learning, task transfer, task selection, natural language processing
problem: Because inter-task relationships are poorly understood, researchers lack principled ways to select helpful source tasks for learning a new target task.
proposed_solution: The authors introduce TaskWeb to benchmark pairwise transfers and propose TaskShop, a method that uses pivot tasks and transfer scores to select source tasks for an unseen target.
claim: TaskShop effectively selects source tasks using pairwise transfer scores, enabling small multi-task training sets to achieve superior zero-shot performance compared to models trained on much larger task sets.
dataset_testbed: TaskWeb, ANLI, CB, QNLI, RTE, SciTail, SNLI, MRPC, QQP, STSB, IMDB, Rotten Tomatoes, COPA, CosmosQA, HellaSwag, PIQA, Quartz, SocialIQA, Winogrande, WiC, WSC, BoolQ, SQuAD2.0, Story Cloze
abstract: Recent work in NLP has shown promising results in training models on large amounts of tasks to achieve better generalization. However, it is not well-understood how tasks are related, and how helpful training tasks can be chosen for a new task. In this work, we investigate whether knowing task relationships via pairwise task transfer improves choosing one or more source tasks that help to learn a new target task. We provide TaskWeb, a large-scale benchmark of pairwise task transfers for 22 NLP tasks using three different model types, sizes, and adaptation methods, spanning about 25,000 experiments. Then, we design a new method TaskShop based on our analysis of TaskWeb. TaskShop uses TaskWeb to estimate the benefit of using a source task for learning a new target task, and to choose a subset of helpful training tasks for multi-task training. Our method improves overall rankings and top-kk precision of source tasks by 10% and 38%, respectively. We also use TaskShop to build much smaller multi-task training sets that improve zero-shot performances across 11 different target tasks by at least 4.3%. 11 1 Our code is available at [https://github.com/danieljkim0118/TaskWeb](https://github.com/danieljkim0118/TaskWeb "").

title: When Does Aggregating Multiple Skills with Multi-Task Learning Work? A Case Study in Financial NLP
venue: Proceedings of the 61st Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics Volume 1: Long Papers
themes: multi-task learning, financial NLP, task aggregation, parameter-efficient fine-tuning
problem: It is unclear when multi-task learning helps, because negative transfer often occurs, and past work studies algorithmic fixes more than which tasks and skills should be aggregated.
proposed_solution: The authors run a case study in Financial NLP where they aggregate six datasets covering diverse skills with multi-task learning and test which aggregation properties make it work.
claim: Aggregating diverse but related Financial NLP tasks with MTL improves most tasks cheaply, provided the aggregation size matches the shared capacity of the model.
dataset_testbed: FinDATA (six-task Financial NLP aggregation compiled by the authors), Financial PhraseBank sentiment classification (SC), SemEval-2017 Task 5 target-based sentiment analysis (TSA), FinNum-3 number classification (NC), FinNum-2 number attachment detection (NAD), TAP quantitative semantic role labeling dataset (FSRL), FinCausal 2020 causality detection (CD), StockSen (unseen task few-shot generalization), Numeracy-600K (unseen task few-shot generalization), NVIDIA RTX2080 GPUs
abstract: Multi-task learning (MTL) aims at achieving a better model by leveraging data and knowledge from multiple tasks. However, MTL does not always work – sometimes negative transfer occurs between tasks, especially when aggregating loosely related skills, leaving it an open question when MTL works. Previous studies show that MTL performance can be improved by algorithmic tricks. However, what tasks and skills should be included is less well explored. In this work, we conduct a case study in Financial NLP where multiple datasets exist for skills relevant to the domain, such as numeric reasoning and sentiment analysis. Due to the task difficulty and data scarcity in the Financial NLP domain, we explore when aggregating such diverse skills from multiple datasets with MTL can work. Our findings suggest that the key to MTL success lies in skill diversity, relatedness between tasks, and choice of aggregation size and shared capacity. Specifically, MTL works well when tasks are diverse but related, and when the size of the task aggregation and the shared capacity of the model are balanced to avoid overwhelming certain tasks.

title: CebuaNER: A New Baseline Cebuano Named Entity Recognition Model
venue: PACLIC 37 (2023)
themes: named entity recognition, low-resource languages, Cebuano, corpus annotation
algorithm_or_model: CebuaNER, a CRF and BiLSTM baseline for Cebuano NER
problem: Cebuano lacks gold-standard named entity recognition data and baseline models because low-resource Southeast Asian languages receive far less research support than high-resource languages.
proposed_solution: The authors collected and annotated 4,258 Cebuano news articles with native speaker annotators, then trained Conditional Random Field and BiLSTM models on this corpus as a public baseline.
claim: The optimized CRF model exceeded 0.70 in precision, recall, and F1 for every entity tag, setting a stronger baseline for Cebuano NER with crosslingual potential.
dataset_testbed: CebuaNER corpus of 4,258 annotated Cebuano news articles from Yes the Best Dumaguete, Filipinas Bisaya, and SunStar Cebu (new dataset), cebtenten Cebuano corpus from Sketch Engine for word cluster features, Corrected Tagalog WikiANN dataset from the calamanCy library with 782 documents for the crosslingual experiment
abstract: Despite being one of the most linguistically diverse groups of countries, computational linguistics and language processing research in Southeast Asia has struggled to match the level of countries from the Global North. Thus, initiatives such as open-sourcing corpora and the development of baseline models for basic language processing tasks are important stepping stones to encourage the growth of research efforts in the field. To answer this call, we introduce CebuaNER, a new baseline model for named entity recognition (NER) in the Cebuano language. Cebuano is the second most-used native language in the Philippines with over 20 million speakers. To build the model, we collected and annotated over 4,000 news articles, the largest of any work in the language, retrieved from online local Cebuano platforms to train algorithms such as Conditional Random Field and Bidirectional LSTM. Our findings show promising results as a new baseline model, achieving over 70% performance on precision, recall, and F1 across all entity tags as well as potential efficacy in a crosslingual setup with Tagalog.

title: Leveraging Multi-Task Learning in Code-Switched setting
venue: Research Square
themes: multi-task learning, code-switching, named entity recognition, natural language processing
algorithm_or_model: Multi-task hard-parameter-sharing architecture of transformer encoder, BiLSTM and shared MLPs with task-specific MLP-CRF layers
problem: NLP systems struggle to interpret code-switched language because models must adapt to language-mixing patterns, and code-switched data is scarce and lacks the transcriptions needed to train deep learning models.
proposed_solution: The authors propose a multi-task learning framework with hard parameter sharing that couples a pre-trained multilingual transformer encoder with a bidirectional LSTM and shared MLP layers, plus task-specific MLP-CRF heads and an uncertainty-weighted joint loss, so that a primary token classification task can benefit from the training signals of a related task.
claim: Multi-task learning in a code-switched setting outperforms the traditional single-task approach, with the NER task leveraging signals from the related language identification task to improve generalizability and F1 performance across all tested pre-trained models.
dataset_testbed: LinCE benchmark (Named Entity Recognition and Language Identification tasks, Hindi-English)
abstract: Multilingualism is the ability to converse fluently in more than one language. In multilingual societies, code-switching, the practise of switching languages during a conversation, occurs often, creating a need for multilingual dialogue and voice recognition systems in natural language processing (NLP). However, interpreting code-switching utterances is extremely difficult for these NLP systems, as the model must adjust to code-switching patterns. In recent years, deep learning strategies have enabled natural language systems with massive volumes of training data to attain human-level performance in languages. However, they cannot accommodate a large number of low-resource languages, mostly mixed languages. Also, code-switching, despite being a common occurrence, is unique to spoken language and lacks the transcriptions necessary for training deep learning models. Our work in this paper, explores the usage of multi-task learning in code-switched setting to see if it can leverage from the training signals of related tasks and improve the generalizability as well as boost the performance and metrics of our model.

title: Recon: Reducing Conflicting Gradients from the Root for Multi-Task Learning
venue: 11th International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2023)
themes: multi-task learning, conflicting gradients, negative transfer, network architecture design
problem: Multi-task learning suffers from negative transfer because task gradients can conflict during joint optimization, allowing dominant gradients to hurt the performance of other tasks and preventing convergence to a good solution.
proposed_solution: The authors propose Recon, which measures layer-wise task gradient conflicts during an initial training run, converts the shared layers with the highest conflict scores into task-specific layers, and retrains the modified network from scratch.
claim: Recon greatly reduces the occurrence of severe conflicting gradients in the remaining shared layers and consistently improves the performance of existing multi-task learning methods while adding only a small number of parameters.
dataset_testbed: Multi-Fashion+MNIST, CityScapes, NYUv2, PASCAL-Context, CelebA
abstract: A fundamental challenge for multi-task learning is that different tasks may conflict with each other when they are solved jointly, and a cause of this phenomenon is *conflicting gradients* during optimization. Recent works attempt to mitigate the influence of conflicting gradients by directly altering the gradients based on some criteria. However, our empirical study shows that “gradient surgery” cannot effectively reduce the occurrence of conflicting gradients. In this paper, we take a different approach to reduce conflicting gradients *from the root*. In essence, we investigate the task gradients w.r.t. each *shared* network layer, select the layers with high conflict scores, and turn them to *task-specific* layers. Our experiments show that such a simple approach can greatly reduce the occurrence of conflicting gradients in the remaining shared layers and achieve better performance, with only a slight increase in model parameters in many cases. Our approach can be easily applied to improve various state-of-the-art methods including gradient manipulation methods and branched architecture search methods. Given a network architecture (e.g., ResNet18), it only needs to search for the conflict layers once, and the network can be modified to be used with different methods on the same or even different datasets to gain performance improvement. The source code is available at [https://github.com/moukamisama/Recon](https://github.com/moukamisama/Recon "").

title: iTANONG-DS : A Collection of Benchmark Datasets for Downstream Natural Language Processing Tasks on Select Philippine Languages
venue: Proceedings of the 2023 International Conference on Natural Language and Speech Processing
themes: benchmark datasets, low-resource languages, Philippine languages, pretrained language models
algorithm_or_model: iTANONG-DS datasets with pretrained BERT and RoBERTa language models
problem: Benchmark datasets for low-resource Philippine languages such as Tagalog and Cebuano are scarce, and existing corpora overrepresent formal text and miss informal everyday usage.
proposed_solution: The authors release iTANONG-DS, unlabeled and labeled datasets for sentiment analysis, part-of-speech tagging, named entity recognition, and language modeling, plus pretrained word embeddings and language models.
claim: The collection closes a resource gap for Tagalog and Cebuano NLP and includes what the authors describe as the first BERT-based language model trained exclusively for Cebuano.
dataset_testbed: iTANONG unlabeled Tagalog and Cebuano corpus scraped from government and media websites, social media, and online forums, iTANONG-DS sentiment analysis dataset with balanced, unbalanced-A, and unbalanced-B subsets, iTANONG-POS part-of-speech tagging dataset with 3,919 tagged sequences, iTANONG-NER dataset with 6,230 data points, HateSpeech dataset by Cruz and Cheng (2022) for sentiment benchmark comparison, WikiAnn NER dataset for benchmark comparison
abstract: Benchmark datasets are crucial for evaluating algorithms and models objectively. They provide a standardized basis for comparisons, promote reproducibility, and drive innovation by establishing baselines and encouraging advancements in the field. Limited benchmark datasets exist for various natural language processing tasks in low-resource languages, including most Philippine languages. As part of iTANONG's 10 billion token dataset initiative, the authors release the first iteration of iTANONG-DS1, a collection of unlabeled and labeled datasets for different NLP tasks such as sentiment analysis, part-of-speech tagging, named entity recognition for Tagalog, and language modeling for Cebuano.

title: HumSet: Dataset of Multilingual Information Extraction and Classification for Humanitarian Crisis Response
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2022
themes: humanitarian crisis response, multilingual NLP, multi-label text classification, information extraction
algorithm_or_model: Fine-tuned multilingual pre-trained Transformer language models, mainly XLM-RBase, alongside XtremeDistil6-h256, fastText, and LEAD4 baselines
problem: Analysts responding to humanitarian crises must manually extract and organize key information from large volumes of text, while existing annotated resources are small and mostly sourced from social media.
proposed_solution: The authors release HumSet, a multilingual set of about 17K humanitarian documents with expert-annotated entries and humanitarian analysis framework labels, and they define entry extraction and multi-label classification tasks with language model baselines.
claim: HumSet offers a large and reliable expert-annotated alternative to social media crisis data, and XLM-RBase gives the strongest baseline results while the tag-rich subpillar categories remain difficult.
dataset_testbed: HumSet
abstract: Timely and effective response to humanitarian crises requires quick and accurate analysis of large amounts of text data – a process that can highly benefit from expert-assisted NLP systems trained on validated and annotated data in the humanitarian response domain. To enable creation of such NLP systems, we introduce and release HumSet, a novel and rich multilingual dataset of humanitarian response documents annotated by experts in the humanitarian response community. The dataset provides documents in three languages (English, French, Spanish) and covers a variety of humanitarian crises from 2018 to 2021 across the globe. For each document, HumSet provides selected snippets (entries) as well as assigned classes to each entry annotated using common humanitarian information analysis frameworks. HumSet also provides novel and challenging entry extraction and multi-label entry classification tasks. In this paper, we take a first step towards approaching these tasks and conduct a set of experiments on Pre-trained Language Models (PLM) to establish strong baselines for future research in this domain.

title: Reasonable Effectiveness of Random Weighting: A Litmus Test for Multi-Task Learning
venue: Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR)
themes: multi-task learning, task balancing, random weighting, optimization
algorithm_or_model: Random Weighting (Random Loss Weighting and Random Gradient Weighting)
problem: Task balancing methods in multi-task learning are only checked against fixed equal weighting, so their true benefit is unclear because basic random weighting experiments were never used as a baseline.
proposed_solution: The paper trains multi-task models with random loss or gradient weights sampled from a distribution each iteration and shows these simple methods match carefully designed balancing strategies.
claim: Random weighting consistently beats equal weighting and performs comparably with state-of-the-art balancing methods, which makes it a necessary baseline for judging new multi-task learning methods.
dataset_testbed: NYUv2, CityScapes, CelebA, Office-31, Office-Home, PAWS-X and Universal Dependencies v2.5 from the XTREME benchmark, NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 GPU
abstract: Multi-Task Learning (MTL) has achieved success in various fields. However, how to balance different tasks to achieve good performance is a key problem. To achieve the task balancing, there are many works to carefully design dynamical loss/gradient weighting strategies but the basic random experiments are ignored to examine their effectiveness. In this paper, we propose the Random Weighting (RW) methods, including Random Loss Weighting (RLW) and Random Gradient Weighting (RGW), where an MTL model is trained with random loss/gradient weights sampled from a distribution. To show the effectiveness and necessity of RW methods, theoretically we analyze the convergence of RW and reveal that RW has a higher probability to escape local minima, resulting in better generalization ability. Empirically, we extensively evaluate the proposed RW methods to compare with twelve state-of-the-art methods on five image datasets and two multilingual problems from the XTREME benchmark to show RW methods can achieve comparable performance with state-of-the-art baselines. Therefore, we think that the RW methods are important baselines for MTL and should attract more attentions.

title: MetaWeighting: Learning to Weight Tasks in Multi-Task Learning
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL 2022
themes: multi-task learning, task weighting, meta learning, text classification
problem: Existing task weighting methods in multi-task learning compute task weights only from training losses and ignore the gap between training loss and generalization loss, which degrades MTL performance.
proposed_solution: The authors propose MetaWeighting, which learns task weights automatically by solving a multi-objective bi-level optimization problem in a learning-to-learn manner so that the weights target generalization performance.
claim: MetaWeighting learns task weights without any predefined heuristic and outperforms all tested baselines on multi-task text classification with both TextCNN and BERT encoders.
dataset_testbed: Amazon product reviews sentiment analysis dataset with 14 binary classification domains (Blitzer et al., 2007), 20 Newsgroups dataset reduced to 16 newsgroups and grouped into four 4-class topic classification tasks, TextCNN encoder with pre-trained GloVe embeddings, pre-trained BERT-base model
abstract: Task weighting, which assigns weights on the including tasks during training, significantly matters the performance of Multi-task Learning (MTL); thus, recently, there has been an explosive interest in it. However, existing task weighting methods assign weights only based on the training loss, while ignoring the gap between the training loss and generalization loss. It degenerates MTL's performance. To address this issue, the present paper proposes a novel task weighting algorithm, which automatically weights the tasks via a learning-to-learn paradigm, referred to as MetaWeighting. Extensive experiments are conducted to validate the superiority of our proposed method in multitask text classification.

title: A Survey of Code-switching: Linguistic and Social Perspectives for Language Technologies
venue: Proceedings of the 59th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics and the 11th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing (Volume 1: Long Papers)
themes: code-switching, multilingualism, language technologies, sociolinguistics
problem: Computational research on code-switching has concentrated on improving methods while largely neglecting the linguistic and social insights about code-switching documented across many languages in the established linguistics literature.
proposed_solution: The authors offer a survey of the linguistics literature on code-switching that reviews structural and functional patterns in European and Indian multilingual contexts and reflects on the key issues this raises for language technologies.
claim: The authors conclude that massive language models still fail to represent diverse code-switching types because of missing training data, robust evaluation benchmarks, and end-to-end systems covering sociolinguistic factors, and that their survey is a step toward mutual benefit for computational scientists and linguists.
dataset_testbed: N/A
abstract: The analysis of data in which multiple languages are represented has gained popularity among computational linguists in recent years. So far, much of this research focuses mainly on the improvement of computational methods and largely ignores linguistic and social aspects of C-S discussed across a wide range of languages within the long-established literature in linguistics. To fill this gap, we offer a survey of code-switching (C-S) covering the literature in linguistics with a reflection on the key issues in language technologies. From the linguistic perspective, we provide an overview of structural and functional patterns of C-S focusing on the literature from European and Indian contexts as highly multilingual areas. From the language technologies perspective, we discuss how massive language models fail to represent diverse C-S types due to lack of appropriate training data, lack of robust evaluation benchmarks for C-S (across multilingual situations and types of C-S) and lack of end-toend systems that cover sociolinguistic aspects of C-S as well. Our survey will be a step towards an outcome of mutual benefit for computational scientists and linguists with a shared interest in multilingualism and C-S.

title: Multilingual Code-Switching for Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Intent Prediction and Slot Filling
venue: MRL Workshop @ EMNLP 2021
themes: zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, intent detection and slot filling, code-switching data augmentation, crisis informatics
algorithm_or_model: Chunk-level multilingual code-switching data augmentation with a jointly trained mBERT model
problem: Multilingual transformers retain representations clustered by language, which hurts zero-shot transfer for joint intent prediction and slot filling when the target language is unknown during training.
proposed_solution: The authors augment English training data with chunk-level multilingual code-switching into random languages to improve the language neutrality of a fine-tuned joint transformer model.
claim: Multilingual code-switching augmentation improved zero-shot intent accuracy by 4.2 percent and slot F1 by 1.8 percent on average without needing the target language during training.
dataset_testbed: MultiATIS++ benchmark dataset, New human-annotated disaster tweet dataset in English and Haitian Creole from the Haiti earthquake, Google Colab K80 GPU, ARGO research computing cluster at George Mason University
abstract: Predicting user intent and detecting the corresponding slots from text are two key problems in Natural Language Understanding (NLU). In the context of zero-shot learning, this task is typically approached by either using representations from pre-trained multilingual transformers such as mBERT, or by machine translating the source data into the known target language and then fine-tuning. Our work focuses on a particular scenario where the target language is unknown during training. To this goal, we propose a novel method to augment the monolingual source data using multilingual code-switching via random translations to enhance a transformer’s language neutrality when fine-tuning it for a downstream task. This method also helps discover novel insights on how code-switching with different language families around the world impact the performance on the target language. Experiments on the benchmark dataset of MultiATIS++ yielded an average improvement of +4.2%+4.2\% in accuracy for intent task and +1.8%+1.8\% in F1 for slot task using our method over the state-of-the-art across 88 different languages11 1 Languages that have different morphological structures compared to English, such as Hindi, Turkish, Chinese, and Japanese, yielded higher benefits.. Furthermore, we present an application of our method for crisis informatics using a new human-annotated tweet dataset of slot filling in English and Haitian Creole, collected during Haiti earthquake disaster22 2 Dataset and implementation available at [https://github.com/jitinkrishnan/Multilingual-ZeroShot-SlotFilling](https://github.com/jitinkrishnan/Multilingual-ZeroShot-SlotFilling "")..

title: A Survey on Multi-Task Learning
venue: IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering
themes: multi-task learning, machine learning, learning theory, deep learning
problem: Individual tasks often have too few labeled examples to train accurate learners on their own, and the fast-growing multi-task learning literature lacks a systematic definition and organization of its models, applications, and theory.
proposed_solution: The authors formally define multi-task learning and survey the field by classifying MTL algorithms into five categories (feature learning, low-rank, task clustering, task relation learning, and decomposition), and additionally review combinations with other learning paradigms, big-data techniques, applications, and theoretical analyses.
claim: Comparisons of representative models on benchmark datasets show that multi-task learning performs better than single-task learning in most cases, verifying the effectiveness of MTL.
dataset_testbed: N/A
abstract: Multi-Task Learning (MTL) is a learning paradigm in machine learning and its aim is to leverage useful information contained in multiple related tasks to help improve the generalization performance of all the tasks. In this paper, we give a survey for MTL from the perspective of algorithmic modeling, applications and theoretical analyses. For algorithmic modeling, we give a definition of MTL and then classify different MTL algorithms into five categories, including feature learning approach, low-rank approach, task clustering approach, task relation learning approach and decomposition approach as well as discussing the characteristics of each approach. In order to improve the performance of learning tasks further, MTL can be combined with other learning paradigms including semi-supervised learning, active learning, unsupervised learning, reinforcement learning, multi-view learning and graphical models. When the number of tasks is large or the data dimensionality is high, we review online, parallel and distributed MTL models as well as dimensionality reduction and feature hashing to reveal their computational and storage advantages. Many real-world applications use MTL to boost their performance and we review representative works in this paper. Finally, we present theoretical analyses and discuss several future directions for MTL.

title: GLUECoS : An Evaluation Benchmark for Code-Switched NLP
venue: Proceedings of the 58th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL 2020)
themes: code-switching, evaluation benchmark, multilingual BERT, cross-lingual word embeddings
problem: Annotated data and standardized multi-task evaluations are scarce for code-switched text, so there has been no comprehensive way to compare embedding and multilingual models across code-switched language understanding tasks.
