proposed_solution: The authors introduce GLUECoS, a GLUE-style benchmark of six code-switched NLP tasks in English-Hindi and English-Spanish, and use it to evaluate cross-lingual word embeddings against multilingual BERT, including a variant further fine-tuned on synthetic and real code-switched text.
claim: Multilingual BERT outperforms cross-lingual word embeddings on every GLUECoS task, and fine-tuning it on synthetic plus a small amount of real code-switched data gives the best results on most tasks, showing multilingual models can be further optimized for code-switching.
dataset_testbed: FIRE 2013 LID dataset (English-Hindi language identification), UD POS code-switched dependency dataset (English-Hindi), FG POS dataset from the ICON 2016 shared task (English-Hindi), IIITH Twitter NER corpus (English-Hindi), SAIL code-mixed sentiment corpus from ICON 2017 (English-Hindi), Code-mixed question answering dataset of Chandu et al. 2018 (English-Hindi), New conversational code-switched NLI dataset (English-Hindi), EMNLP 2014 LID shared task dataset (English-Spanish), Bangor Miami corpus (English-Spanish POS tagging), CALCS 2018 NER shared task corpus (English-Spanish), English-Spanish Twitter sentiment corpus of Vilares et al. 2016, IITB English-Hindi parallel corpus used to generate synthetic code-switched data, Twitter and internal parallel corpora used to train cross-lingual embeddings
abstract: Code-switching is the use of more than one language in the same conversation or utterance. Recently, multilingual contextual embedding models, trained on multiple monolingual corpora, have shown promising results on cross-lingual and multilingual tasks. We present an evaluation benchmark, GLUECoS, for code-switched languages, that spans several NLP tasks in English-Hindi and English-Spanish. Specifically, our evaluation benchmark includes Language Identification from text, POS tagging, Named Entity Recognition, Sentiment Analysis, Question Answering and a new task for code-switching, Natural Language Inference. We present results on all these tasks using cross-lingual word embedding models and multilingual models. In addition, we fine-tune multilingual models on artificially generated code-switched data. Although multilingual models perform significantly better than cross-lingual models, our results show that in most tasks, across both language pairs, multilingual models fine-tuned on code-switched data perform best, showing that multilingual models can be further optimized for code-switching tasks.

title: Which Tasks Should Be Learned Together in Multi-task Learning?
venue: Proceedings of the 37th International Conference on Machine Learning
themes: multi-task learning, computer vision, task grouping, task relationships
algorithm_or_model: Task grouping framework with branch-and-bound network selection
problem: Competing task objectives in multi-task networks cause negative transfer, making it unclear which tasks should be grouped together under an inference budget.
proposed_solution: The authors propose a task grouping framework that evaluates candidate task subsets and selects network assignments that minimize total loss within a computational budget.
claim: Assigning tasks to multiple networks based on compatibility consistently achieves lower total loss across computational budgets than either a single multi-task network or independent single-task networks.
dataset_testbed: Taskonomy dataset
abstract: Many computer vision applications require solving multiple tasks in real-time. A neural network can be trained to solve multiple tasks simultaneously using _multi-task learning_ . This can save computation at inference time as only a single network needs to be evaluated. Unfortunately, this often leads to inferior overall performance as task objectives can compete, which consequently poses the question: **which tasks should and should not be learned together in one network when employing multi-task learning?** We study task cooperation and competition in several different learning settings and propose a framework for assigning tasks to a few neural networks such that cooperating tasks are computed by the same neural network, while competing tasks are computed by different networks. Our framework offers a time-accuracy trade-off and can produce better accuracy using less inference time than not only a single large multi-task neural network but also many single-task networks.

title: Weakly-supervised Fine-grained Event Recognition on Social Media Texts for Disaster Management
venue: AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
themes: weak supervision, event recognition, social media mining, disaster management
algorithm_or_model: multi-channel BiLSTM classifier with clustering-assisted word sense disambiguation labeling
problem: Supervised training of fine-grained event recognizers for individual disaster tweets needs large manually labeled datasets that take days to create, which is too slow for time-critical disaster response.
proposed_solution: The approach clusters keyword-matched tweets so an expert can quickly confirm pertinent word senses, then trains a multi-channel BiLSTM using context and reply tweets, and improves coverage through bootstrapping.
claim: Using only 1 to 2 person-hours of labeling effort, the weakly supervised classifiers outperform supervised classifiers trained on more than ten thousand tweets that took over 50 person-hours to annotate.
dataset_testbed: Hurricane Harvey Twitter dataset (about 65k unlabeled tweets and 11,782 annotated evaluation tweets collected via the GNIP API), Hurricane Florence Twitter dataset (about 69.8k unlabeled tweets and 4,059 annotated evaluation tweets collected via the GNIP API), NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1080 GPU
abstract: People increasingly use social media to report emergencies, seek help or share information during disasters, which makes social networks an important tool for disaster management. To meet these time-critical needs, we present a weakly supervised approach for rapidly building high-quality classifiers that label each individual Twitter message with fine-grained event categories. Most importantly, we propose a novel method to create high-quality labeled data in a timely manner that automatically clusters tweets containing an event keyword and asks a domain expert to disambiguate event word senses and label clusters quickly. In addition, to process extremely noisy and often rather short user-generated messages, we enrich tweet representations using preceding context tweets and reply tweets in building event recognition classifiers. The evaluation on two hurricanes, Harvey and Florence, shows that using only 1-2 person-hours of human supervision, the rapidly trained weakly supervised classifiers outperform supervised classifiers trained using more than ten thousand annotated tweets created in over 50 person-hours.

title: I-AID: Identifying Actionable Information from Disaster-related Tweets
venue: IEEE Access
themes: multi-label text classification, crisis informatics, social media analysis, meta learning
problem: Classifying disaster tweets into fine-grained categories is difficult because tweets are noisy, lack sufficient contextual information, and often belong to multiple labels simultaneously.
proposed_solution: The authors propose I-AID, a framework that combines a BERT encoder, a graph attention network for label correlation, and a relation network for distance metric learning.
claim: I-AID outperforms state of the art baselines in weighted F1 score across both crisis datasets and achieves a positive Accumulated Alert Worth score on high priority tweets.
dataset_testbed: TREC-IS, COVID-19 Tweets
abstract: Social media plays a significant role in disaster management by providing valuable data about affected people, donations and help requests. Recent studies highlight the need to filter information on social media into fine-grained content labels. However, identifying useful information from massive amounts of social media posts during a crisis is a challenging task. In this paper, we propose I-AID, a multimodel approach to automatically categorize tweets into multi-label information types and filter critical information from the enormous volume of social media data. I-AID incorporates three main components: i) a BERT-based encoder to capture the semantics of a tweet and represent as a low-dimensional vector, ii) a graph attention network (GAT) to apprehend correlations between tweets’ words/entities and the corresponding information types, and iii) a Relation Network as a learnable distance metric to compute the similarity between tweets and their corresponding information types in a supervised way. We conducted several experiments on two real publicly-available datasets. Our results indicate that I-AID outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in terms of weighted average F1 score by +6%+6\% and +4%+4\% on the TREC-IS dataset and COVID-19 Tweets, respectively.

title: Sentiment Analysis of Typhoon Related Tweets using Standard and Bidirectional Recurrent Neural Networks
venue: Proceedings of the 14th National Natural Language Processing Research Symposium - Student Research Workshop
themes: sentiment analysis, recurrent neural networks, Twitter, natural disaster response
algorithm_or_model: Standard and bidirectional Recurrent Neural Networks
problem: Despite Filipinos producing vast amounts of tweets during natural disasters, very little research has tapped this data to understand the emotions Filipinos express on Twitter during calamities such as Typhoon Yolanda.
proposed_solution: The authors collect and preprocess Typhoon Yolanda related Filipino tweets, manually annotate a balanced sample of 3,900 tweets as positive, negative, or neutral, and train standard and bidirectional recurrent neural networks with Word2Vec features and varied hyperparameters to classify sentiment before, during, and after the typhoon.
claim: Both standard and bidirectional RNNs proved effective for typhoon-related tweet sentiment analysis, scoring above 80% on all evaluation metrics with best accuracies of 81.79% for fine-grained and 87.69% for binary classification, and applying the trained model to the full dataset revealed that 51.1% of tweets were positive, 19.8% negative, and 29% neutral.
dataset_testbed: Typhoon Yolanda related Filipino tweets collected from Twitter (39,867 preprocessed tweets; 3,900 manually annotated)
abstract: The Philippines is a common ground to natural calamities like typhoons, floods, volcanic eruptions and earthquakes. With Twitter as one of the most used social media platform in the Philippines, a total of 39,867 preprocessed tweets were obtained given a time frame starting from November 1, 2013 to January 31, 2014. Sentiment analysis determines the underlying emotion given a series of words. The main purpose of this study is to identify the sentiments expressed in the tweets sent by the Filipino people before, during, and after Typhoon Yolanda using two variations of Recurrent Neural Networks; standard and bidirectional. The best generated models after training with various hyperparameters achieved a high accuracy of 81.79% for fine-grained classification using standard RNN and 87.69% for binary classification using bidirectional RNN. Findings revealed that 51.1% of the tweets sent were positive expressing support, love, and words of courage to the victims; 19.8% were negative stating sadness and despair for the loss of lives and hate for corrupt officials; while the other 29% were neutral tweets from local news stations, announcements of relief operations, donation drives, and observations by citizens.

title: Low-supervision urgency detection and transfer in short crisis messages
venue: Proceedings of the 2019 IEEE/ACM International Conference on Advances in Social Networks Analysis and Mining (ASONAM)
themes: crisis informatics, urgency detection, transfer learning, low-supervision machine learning
algorithm_or_model: Weighted ensemble of three linear regression classifiers over manual, local fastText, and pre-trained Wikipedia embedding features, with an up-sampled source-target transfer variant
problem: Detecting urgent needs in short social media messages during humanitarian crises is hard because only a handful of labeled examples exist when a disaster strikes, each disaster has different characteristics, and social media text is noisy.
proposed_solution: The authors build an urgency classifier from a few hundred labeled tweets by combining manual keyword features, locally trained fastText embeddings, and pre-trained Wikipedia embeddings in a weighted ensemble, and add a transfer variant that trains the ensemble on pooled source and target labeled data with the target up-sampled when no background corpus exists for the new crisis.
claim: The ensemble and transfer learning approaches beat single-feature-set baselines with high statistical significance across the three disaster datasets, with the best low-supervision result being 69.44% F-Measure on Nepal.
dataset_testbed: Nepal earthquake tweet dataset (DARPA LORELEI), Macedonia live-action disaster simulation dataset (DARPA LORELEI), Kerala floods tweet dataset
abstract: Humanitarian disasters have been on the rise in recent years due to the effects of climate change and socio-political situations such as the refugee crisis. Technology can be used to best mobilize resources such as food and water in the event of a natural disaster, by semi-automatically flagging tweets and short messages as indicating an urgent need. The problem is challenging not just because of the sparseness of data in the immediate aftermath of a disaster, but because of the varying characteristics of disasters in developing countries (making it difficult to train just one system) and the noise and quirks in social media. In this paper, we present a robust, low-supervision social media urgency system that adapts to arbitrary crises by leveraging both labeled and unlabeled data in an ensemble setting. The system is also able to adapt to new crises where an unlabeled background corpus may not be available yet by utilizing a simple and effective transfer learning methodology. Experimentally, our transfer learning and low-supervision approaches are found to outperform viable baselines with high significance on myriad disaster datasets.

title: Multi-Task Deep Neural Networks for Natural Language Understanding
venue: Proceedings of the 57th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL 2019)
themes: multi-task learning, natural language understanding, language model pretraining, domain adaptation
problem: Supervised learning of deep neural networks for individual natural language understanding tasks requires large amounts of task-specific labeled data that is often unavailable, and the resulting representations tend to overfit to a single task and generalize poorly to new tasks and domains.
proposed_solution: The authors combine multi-task learning with language model pre-training by extending the MT-DNN architecture to use a pre-trained BERT bidirectional Transformer as shared text-encoding layers, with task-specific output layers trained jointly across many NLU tasks via mini-batch SGD.
claim: MT-DNN achieved new state-of-the-art results on ten NLU tasks, pushing the GLUE benchmark to 82.7% (a 2.2% absolute improvement over BERT_LARGE) and reaching 91.6% on SNLI and 95.0% on SciTail, while its learned representations enabled domain adaptation with substantially fewer in-domain labels than pre-trained BERT.
dataset_testbed: GLUE benchmark (CoLA, SST-2, MNLI, RTE, WNLI, QQP, MRPC, STS-B, QNLI), SNLI, SciTail
abstract: In this paper, we present a Multi-Task Deep Neural Network (MT-DNN) for learning representations across multiple natural language understanding (NLU) tasks. MT-DNN not only leverages large amounts of cross-task data, but also benefits from a regularization effect that leads to more general representations to help adapt to new tasks and domains. MT-DNN extends the model proposed in [Liu et al. (2015)](#bib.bib16 "") by incorporating a pre-trained bidirectional transformer language model, known as BERT ([Devlin et al., 2018](#bib.bib6 "")). MT-DNN obtains new state-of-the-art results on ten NLU tasks, including SNLI, SciTail, and eight out of nine GLUE tasks, pushing the GLUE benchmark to 82.7% (2.2% absolute improvement) 11 1 As of February 25, 2019 on the latest GLUE test set.. We also demonstrate using the SNLI and SciTail datasets that the representations learned by MT-DNN allow domain adaptation with substantially fewer in-domain labels than the pre-trained BERT representations. The code and pre-trained models are publicly available at https://github.com/namisan/mt-dnn.

title: GLUE: A Multi-Task Benchmark and Analysis Platform for Natural Language Understanding
venue: 7th International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2019)
themes: natural language understanding, multi-task learning, benchmark evaluation, transfer learning
algorithm_or_model: multi-task BiLSTM sentence encoder with attention and ELMo/CoVe transfer learning
problem: Most NLU models are built for one specific task and generalize poorly across tasks and domains, and before this work the field lacked a unified benchmark for measuring genuinely general language understanding.
proposed_solution: The authors assemble GLUE, a benchmark of nine existing sentence- and sentence-pair-level NLU tasks served through an online evaluation platform, together with a hand-crafted diagnostic dataset, and deliberately include low-resource tasks so that strong models must share linguistic knowledge across tasks.
claim: Multi-task training on all GLUE tasks, especially when combined with attention and ELMo, outperforms per-task training and pretrained sentence encoders, yet the best model's absolute scores remain low enough that GLUE stays beyond the reach of the then-current methods.
dataset_testbed: CoLA (Corpus of Linguistic Acceptability), SST-2 (Stanford Sentiment Treebank), MRPC (Microsoft Research Paraphrase Corpus), QQP (Quora Question Pairs), STS-B (Semantic Textual Similarity Benchmark), MNLI (Multi-Genre Natural Language Inference Corpus), QNLI (Question-answering NLI, derived from SQuAD), RTE (combined RTE1, RTE2, RTE3, and RTE5), WNLI (Winograd NLI), GLUE diagnostic dataset (new hand-crafted NLI analysis set created by this paper), SNLI (used as 550k examples of auxiliary training data for MNLI)
abstract: For natural language understanding (NLU) technology to be maximally useful, it must be able to process language in a way that is not exclusive to a single task, genre, or dataset. In pursuit of this objective, we introduce the General Language Understanding Evaluation (GLUE) benchmark, a collection of tools for evaluating the performance of models across a diverse set of existing NLU tasks. By including tasks with limited training data, GLUE is designed to favor and encourage models that share general linguistic knowledge across tasks. GLUE also includes a hand-crafted diagnostic test suite that enables detailed linguistic analysis of models. We evaluate baselines based on current methods for transfer and representation learning and find that multi-task training on all tasks performs better than training a separate model per task. However, the low absolute performance of our best model indicates the need for improved general NLU systems.

title: A Joint Many-Task Model: Growing a Neural Network for Multiple NLP Tasks
venue: Proceedings of the 2017 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP 2017)
themes: multi-task learning, transfer learning, recurrent neural networks, natural language processing
problem: Multi-task NLP models typically address only few related tasks and ignore linguistic hierarchies because they predict outputs at the same layer or in isolated pipelines.
proposed_solution: The authors present a joint many-task model that stacks recurrent layers for increasingly complex linguistic tasks and uses shortcut connections with successive regularization.
claim: The single end-to-end JMT model outperforms single-task baselines across all five tasks and achieves state-of-the-art or competitive results on chunking, parsing, relatedness, and entailment.
dataset_testbed: Wall Street Journal portion of Penn Treebank (POS tagging), Wall Street Journal corpus with CoNLL-2000 split (chunking), Wall Street Journal corpus with Stanford dependencies (dependency parsing), SICK dataset (semantic relatedness and textual entailment), English Wikipedia text (embedding pre-training)
abstract: Transfer and multi-task learning have traditionally focused on either a single source-target pair or very few, similar tasks. Ideally, the linguistic levels of morphology, syntax and semantics would benefit each other by being trained in a single model. We introduce a joint many-task model together with a strategy for successively growing its depth to solve increasingly complex tasks. Higher layers include shortcut connections to lower-level task predictions to reflect linguistic hierarchies. We use a simple regularization term to allow for optimizing all model weights to improve one task’s loss without exhibiting catastrophic interference of the other tasks. Our single end-to-end model obtains state-of-the-art or competitive results on five different tasks from tagging, parsing, relatedness, and entailment tasks.

title: Disaster Response Aided by Tweet Classification with a Domain Adaptation Approach
venue: Journal of Contingencies and Crisis Management
themes: domain adaptation, disaster response, tweet classification, naive bayes
algorithm_or_model: weighted Naïve Bayes domain adaptation with iterative self-training (NB-ST)
problem: Supervised classifiers learned from one disaster perform poorly on a new disaster because each event produces unique social media responses, and labeled data for the new event is unavailable.
proposed_solution: The authors adapt a weighted Naïve Bayes domain adaptation algorithm that uses self-training with hard labels to combine source labeled tweets with target unlabeled tweets.
claim: Domain adaptation classifiers beat supervised classifiers trained only on source data, with self-training generally better than expectation maximization, and results close to an ideal classifier trained on labeled target data.
dataset_testbed: CrisisLexT6 dataset of tweets from six disasters (Olteanu et al., 2014), Beocat Research Cluster at Kansas State University
abstract: Social media platforms such as Twitter provide valuable information for aiding disaster response during emergency events. Machine learning could be used to identify such information. However, supervised learning algorithms rely on labeled data, which is not readily available for an emerging target disaster. While labeled data might be available for a prior source disaster, supervised classifiers learned only from the source disaster may not perform well on the target disaster, as each event has unique characteristics (e.g., type, location, culture) and may cause different social media responses. To address this limitation, we propose to use a domain adaptation approach, which learns classifiers from unlabeled target data, in addition to source labeled data. Our approach uses the Naïve Bayes classifier, together with an iterative Self-­Training strategy. Experimental results on the task of identifying tweets relevant to a disaster of interest show that the domain adaptation classifiers are better as compared to the supervised classifiers learned only from labeled source data.

title: Robust Classification of Crisis-Related Data on Social Networks Using Convolutional Neural Networks
venue: Proceedings of the Eleventh International AAAI Conference on Web and Social Media (ICWSM 2017)
themes: crisis informatics, tweet classification, convolutional neural networks, word embeddings
problem: Supervised classifiers for detecting useful crisis tweets need event-specific labeled data, which is scarce in the early hours of a disaster when it is needed most.
proposed_solution: The authors classify tweets with a convolutional neural network that learns features from word embeddings and can reuse labeled data from past crises when new event labels are missing.
claim: Convolutional neural networks classified crisis tweets more reliably than non-neural classifiers in all training settings and gave reasonable predictions from out-of-event data when no event labels existed.
dataset_testbed: CrisisNLP dataset of human-labeled crisis tweets, CrisisLex dataset of human-labeled crisis tweets, AIDR dataset of volunteer-labeled crisis tweets, 300-dimensional Google News word2vec embeddings, Crisis embeddings trained with word2vec skip-gram on 57,908 disaster tweets
abstract: The role of social media, in particular microblogging platforms such as Twitter, as a conduit for actionable and tactical information during disasters is increasingly acknowledged. However, time-critical analysis of big crisis data on social media streams brings challenges to machine learning techniques, especially the ones that use supervised learning. The scarcity of labeled data, particularly in the early hours of a crisis, delays the learning process. Existing classification methods require a significant amount of labeled data specific to a particular event for training plus a lot of feature engineering to achieve best results. In this work, we introduce neural network based classification methods for identifying useful tweets during a crisis situation. At the onset of a disaster when no labeled data is available, our proposed method makes the best use of the out-of-event data and achieves good results.

title: An Overview of Multi-Task Learning in Deep Neural Networks
venue: arXiv
themes: multi-task learning, deep neural networks, transfer learning, auxiliary tasks
problem: Models trained in isolation on a single task ignore the training signals of related tasks, which could otherwise help them generalize better on the metric they care about.
proposed_solution: The author surveys multi-task learning in deep neural networks, introducing hard and soft parameter sharing, the mechanisms that explain why MTL works, recent architectures that learn what to share, and guidelines for choosing auxiliary tasks.
claim: Sharing representations across related tasks improves generalization, and while hard parameter sharing remains the dominant paradigm for neural multi-task learning, recent methods that learn what to share are promising and generally outperform it.
dataset_testbed: N/A
abstract: Multi-task learning (MTL) has led to successes in many applications of machine learning, from natural language processing and speech recognition to computer vision and drug discovery. This article aims to give a general overview of MTL, particularly in deep neural networks. It introduces the two most common methods for MTL in Deep Learning, gives an overview of the literature, and discusses recent advances. In particular, it seeks to help ML practitioners apply MTL by shedding light on how MTL works and providing guidelines for choosing appropriate auxiliary tasks.

title: Design Science in Information Systems Research
venue: MIS Quarterly
themes: design science, information systems research methodology, design evaluation, IT artifacts
algorithm_or_model: Information Systems research framework and seven design-science research guidelines
problem: Information systems research lacks clear standards for design science, which makes it hard to distinguish design research from routine system building.
proposed_solution: The authors propose a conceptual framework combining design science and behavioral science, supported by seven practical guidelines for conducting and evaluating design-science research.
claim: The authors argue that both design science and behavioral science are essential to ensure the rigor, relevance, and effectiveness of information systems research.
dataset_testbed: N/A
abstract: Two paradigms characterize much of the research in the Information Systems discipline:  behavioral science and design science.  The behavioralscience paradigm seeks to develop and verify theories that explain or predict human or organizational behavior.  The design-science paradigm seeks to extend the boundaries of human and organizational capabilities by creating new and innovative artifacts.  Both paradigms are foundational to the IS discipline, positioned as it is at the confluence of people, organizations, and technology.  Our objective is to describe the performance of design-science research in Information Systems via a concise conceptual framework and clear guidelines for understanding, executing, and evaluating the research.   In the design-science paradigm, knowledge and understanding of a problem domain and its solution are achieved in the building and application of the designed artifact.  Three recent exemplars in the research literature are used to demonstrate the application of these guidelines.  We conclude with an analysis of the challenges of performing high-quality design-science research in the context of the broader IS community.

title: The Measurement of Observer Agreement for Categorical Data
venue: Biometrics
themes: inter-rater reliability, kappa, observer agreement interpretation
algorithm_or_model: Generalized kappa-type statistics with interpretation bands
problem: Annotation quality needs an accepted standard for interpreting observer agreement coefficients.
proposed_solution: Interpret kappa in bands, slight, fair, moderate, substantial, and almost perfect.
claim: The bands remain the standard convention for characterizing kappa strength.
dataset_testbed: N/A
abstract: This paper presents a general statistical methodology for the analysis of multivariate categorical data arising from observer reliability studies. The procedure essentially involves the construction of functions of the observed proportions which are directed at the extent to which the observers agree among themselves and the construction of test statistics for hypotheses involving these functions. Tests for interobserver bias are presented in terms of first-order marginal homogeneity and measures of interobserver agreement are developed as generalized kappa-type statistics. These procedures are illustrated with a clinical diagnosis example from the epidemiological literature.
